cases.case_text:

On examination, she had hepatomegaly and tenderness in the right hypochondrium.

annotation.title: Role of cytology in fibroadenoma with clinging carcinoma

cases.case_text:
A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

annotation.title: Difficult diagnosis of brainstem glioblastoma multiforme in a woman: a case report and review of the literature

cases.case_text:
A 48-year-old otherwise healthy woman presented with a 5-day history of headache, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination and laboratory tests were within normal limits. She was diagnosed with tension headache and sinusitis and discharged on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Three days later, her headache had resolved but vomiting persisted twice daily; she was treated with an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor for suspected gastroesophageal reflux. Over the following week, she developed ataxia, diplopia, and recurrence of her headache. 

She presented to the emergency department, and a T2-weighted MRI of the head showed increased signaling of the left temporal lobe, bilateral pontine regions, left peridentate nucleus, and cervical spinal cord. These findings were thought to represent an acute demyelinating process. Clinical suspicion for myasthenia gravis was high, and she was administered a trial of pyridostigmine without improvement. During hospitalization, her blood pressure rose to 190/90 mmHg, serum sodium was 123 mEq/L, glucose 176 mg/dL, and white-cell count 12,800 cells/mL. Neurologically, she had decreased sensorium, hallucinations, diminished attention span, and gait disturbance. A lumbar puncture showed an elevated opening pressure. 

Based on radiographic, laboratory, and clinical findings, a diagnosis of acute demyelinating encephalopathy was made, and suspicions of infectious encephalitis, collagen vascular disease, and toxic encephalitis were high. She received plasmapheresis without improvement. A follow-up T2-weighted MRI showed progressive enlargement of the bilateral pontine regions with hydrocephalus and mass effect on the fourth ventricle. A 74-year-old Caucasian woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed in 2006, complex karyotype with TP53 mutation and trisomy 12) was receiving zanubrutinib and subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement for hypogammaglobulinemia. annotation.title: An Unusual Presentation of Catatonia-Like Behavior: Differentiating Malingering from Catatonia

cases.case_text:
A 45-year-old woman was admitted to an acute psychiatric hospital with depressed mood, suicidal ideation, and auditory hallucinations. She had been discharged five days earlier from another facility and had 18 emergency department visits in the prior year. Her psychiatric history included benzodiazepine use disorder, opiate use disorder, borderline personality disorder, and major depressive disorder. Home medications were clonazepam, clonidine, buprenorphine–naloxone, fluoxetine, gabapentin, and trazodone. She was unemployed, homeless, and without family support.

During the admission, she exhibited:
- Catatonia-like signs: flat affect with psychomotor retardation and fluctuating mutism; complete lack of social contact; twitching, eye grimacing, and shoulder shrugging; posturing and immobility; diaphoresis.
- Psychotic signs: mouthing words and seemingly responding to internal stimuli; thought blocking; reported auditory hallucinations.
- Seizure-like behavior: episodes of head jerking with eye fluttering without tongue biting; remained conversant; benign neurologic examination.

Clues suggesting volitional behavior included selective acceptance of benzodiazepines and gabapentin while refusing other medications, eating all meals despite “stupor,” abruptly lapsing into and out of catatonia-like and psychotic behaviors depending on the topic of conversation, purposeful movements to obtain lorazepam after seizures, and evidence of self‐induced urinary incontinence during one episode.

A regional catatonia specialist evaluated her and noted that she was unlikely to have catatonia. Repeated lorazepam challenge tests had limited effect on her behaviors and appeared to reinforce them.

G. Malingering was most likely

cases.case_text:
A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. 

On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. 

Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. cases.case_text:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

A 46-year-old Japanese woman with a history of epilepsy presented with redness and swelling of the right breast. On examination, there was erythema and swelling in the lower right breast. Ultrasound revealed a 54 × 41 × 31 mm low-echo mass with partially unclear margins in the outer right breast. Biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type), high grade, ER+, PgR–, HER2 3+, Ki67 70%. Whole-body PET-CT revealed increased uptake in the right axilla, anterior mediastinum, left pleura, and liver, consistent with cT4dN3M1 stage IV breast cancer.
